item.content:encoded:
In short:
Almost all women surveyed in a new Australian study reported encountering harmful behaviour on dating apps, with many taking their own precautions to stay safe.
Researchers say platforms should do more to prevent systemic risks as the federal government considers a digital duty of care.
What's next?
Consultation on Labor's proposed digital duty of care closes on Tuesday, with advocates saying it has capacity to curb online abuse.
Women are being forced to act as their own safety system on dating apps where experiences of sexual harassment, manipulation and controlling behaviours are widespread, a study has found.
Australian researchers found 99 per cent of heterosexual women surveyed had encountered at least one harmful behaviour on a dating app in the previous three months.
Unsolicited explicit messages, attempts to monitor activity, love bombing, negging and gaslighting are common experiences on dating apps, according to the study released on Tuesday by the Minderoo Foundation-funded Behaviour Insights Team (BIT).
Women reported routinely screening profiles for warning signs, withholding identifying information and carefully managing interactions to protect themselves from potential harm.
These accounts have fuelled calls to ensure a proposed digital duty of care was implemented to require online services to tackle systemic risks.
Researchers have argued the scale of the problem showed women could not be expected to manage the risks alone, with dating platforms better placed to prevent harm before it occurred.
Women coaching each other to stay safe
Brisbane resident Rebecca Wilson, 33, said her harmful dating app experiences have included receiving "completely unsolicited" and "aggressively sexual" messages, photos and videos.
Ms Wilson said she was also once stalked by a man she had met via an app.
"We went on one date. I said to him, 'Look I'm just not interested anymore', and he didn't get the message," she said.
"Weeks later he kept popping up at the same places as me … following me around.
"He touched me at a bar right in front of my friends when it was clearly unsolicited."
With only minimal information on the man, Ms Wilson said she could not easily report him to authorities.
One issue was that using the "block" feature on the app meant she lost the ability to collect identifying material to progress a complaint.
"There's no way of being able to know the identity of who you were talking to," Ms WIlson said.
Ms Wilson said she and her friends have "coached" each other through how to navigate online dating safely.
"The current mechanisms are really just not enough on these apps," she said.
Harmful behaviour 'normalised'
The most common harmful behaviours on dating apps were psychological and emotional, which were encountered by 95 per cent of the 1,008 women across Australia surveyed for the BIT study.
About 89 per cent experienced monitoring and surveillance activity and 88 per cent reported being sent unsolicited sexual images and videos, and being pressured and manipulated into sending sexual content.
Almost six in 10 women reported fear-based controlling behaviour, including threats of physical harm. Of those, only about 22 per cent reported those threats to the platforms.
Among women who made reports to platforms generally, about 19 per cent felt their complaint was "barely" or "not at all" taken seriously, while 64 per cent said they were taken at least "somewhat" seriously.
Lead researcher Karen Tindall said the findings showed there was a need for greater efforts by the platforms to tackle "genuinely preventable risk".
"Right now, a lot of these behaviours are so normalised that women blame themselves or they think they are overreacting," she said.
"This data and research should validate women's experience and should shift the conversation toward fixing the system itself."
Dr Tindall said there were features built for safety that could lead to harm, such as preventing screenshots to prevent against image-based abuse.
"But that also removes a woman's ability to document what happened," she said.
"I'm not saying those safety features should be removed, but it means that safety features need to be tested for how they will be worked around, and whether they will work as intended."
Duty would shift responsibility onto platforms
The findings have been released as the federal government consults on its proposed digital duty of care, which is intended to require services to identify and mitigate foreseeable risks rather than relying on users to report harm after the fact.
The draft duty for adults could apply to dating platforms on which users have faced serious abuse, stalking, sexual violence or image-based abuse.
It would mean services were required to identify and mitigate systemic risks that could enable such conduct.
While the initial debate has focused on social media, the proposed duty would apply more broadly across digital services, including dating and messaging apps, online games, search engines and AI services.
Minderoo Foundation gender equality executive director Jacqueline Joudo Larsen said a digital duty of care could prevent harm and protect Australians.
"It is the single biggest lever to curb the reach, scale and speed at which abuse is occurring by shifting responsibility from individuals to companies that are designing and operating online platforms," she said.
"This is a standard that we hold other sectors to and it should be no different for the online space."
Ms Larsen said technology had "transformed" how people met, connected and built relationships.
"Those benefits are very meaningful," she said.
"But safety cannot be the price women pay for participation.
"This is a design problem that's entirely preventable."
Ms Larsen said Australia could be a leader in tech safety and, if it was serious about ending sexual and domestic violence, that was an "opportunity we can't squander".
Labor's proposal under scrutiny
Submissions on Labor's proposal close on Tuesday and draft legislation will likely be introduced next month.
The Coalition has criticised the draft, primarily due to concerns over discretionary powers allowing the minister to add additional "harms" for children and "serious harms" for adults.
In a social media post shared by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, the Coalition dubbed the idea the "Albo-rithm" and suggested the government would seek to censor online spaces.
But Communications Minister Anika Wells has repeatedly said the intent of the rule making power was about acting with "urgency" if new threats, such as apps that allowed users to "nudify" photos, arose online.
"We think this is a sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming online every single day," she said earlier this month.
The discretion in the bill for adding additional harms would be disallowable by the Senate at any time, but Labor might have to make some changes to their plan in order to secure the Greens' support for the draft bill.
In another submission to the draft legislation, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman has described the reforms as a "rare opportunity" to build trust and accountability into the digital economy from the outset.
Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said trust would not be built by hoping companies did the right thing and urged the government to consider an independent external dispute mechanism for when system failures occurred.
"Everyday Australians need someone to turn to for support holding big tech companies accountable when they get things wrong and we stand ready to help," she said.
The submission said an external complaints system would provide a "practical avenue" for Australians to resolve issues such as restoration of account access, ensuring choices about algorithms are implemented and reconsidering incorrect decisions.

Passionate Northampton fundraiser branches out to host crafters carousel workshop – think speed dating but with crafts
A passionate fundraiser in Northampton has branched out to host a new style of event called a crafters carousel workshop, which she has described as speed dating but with crafts.
Natalie Wood is known for organising charity events in memory of her late brother Sam Grove. These raise money and awareness for Northamptonshire Mind to support mental health and address the stigma around alcohol addiction.
Sam tragically passed away at the age of 30 in March 2023 and Natalie has organised multiple successful community events, including a winter shopping experience at The Elgar Centre and summer gatherings at The George Inn.
Natalie has now broadened her horizons to host events under the umbrella organisation of Natalie Wood Events, and the crafters carousel workshop is taking place from 10am until 1pm on October 18 at The Brampton Halt.
This will be a relaxed morning when attendees will get to try four different crafts with a brilliant group of makers. You will spend 30 minutes at each station before moving onto the next, and you do not need to consider yourself crafty to come along.
This is an introductory and experimental workshop, with a focus on simply having a go, trying something new and seeing what you enjoy.
The first station will be needle felting with Ali Edwards from Fuzzycrumbs, during which attendees will make a small pumpkin from 100 percent wool. The next is centred around essential oils and making your own roller ball with Sabrina Smart.
Kerry Mattock Tobin from Kerry’s Creative Therapeutic Workshops will help the crafters get hands on with clay, and Lizzie Foster from Hoglet House Crafts will be teaching the basics of paper quilling.
Because no morning of crafting is complete without refreshments, there will be cakes and drinks too. Tickets are £30 per person and include the four taster sessions, all the materials you need, your creations to take home, and the chance to try something outside of your comfort zone.
There will also be the opportunity to purchase some of the crafters’ kits to take away, so if you discover something you love, you can carry on creating at home. Spaces are limited so secure your ticket while they are still available.

item.content:encoded:
Dating in Lahore is an entire sport in itself. You have to pick the right coffee shop, the right corner, the right time of day, preferably somewhere your mother’s friend is unlikely to walk in, and pray the weather doesn’t ruin the outfit you spent an hour choosing.
Step inside any air-conditioned hipster café and you’ll spot them immediately. At least three couples tucked into corner booths, oblivious to the September heat, holding hands, or spoon-feeding each other tres leches cake while the staff desperately looks anywhere else.
Psychiatrist John Bowlby noted in his work on attachment theory that our drive for deep intimacy is a lot more than a nice-to-have. It’s an instinctual imperative. He observed that most intense human emotions are sparked during the formation, maintenance, and disruption of romantic bonds.
But it’s no secret that in Pakistan, instinctual imperative collides with cultural veto. Outside of a few ultra cosmopolitan bubble zones in Lahore, dating is policed by a rigid mix of religious norms and cultural scrutiny for consenting young adults.
To explore this weird, wonderful, and deeply neurotic dynamic, I polled 34 anonymous Lahoris navigating the city’s covert romance scene. I asked them two simple questions:
-
Is dating in Lahore difficult? Why?
-
How do you deal with the weight of secrecy, guilt, conservative judgment, or moral hesitation that may come with it?
Despite growing up on Bollywood’s grand declarations of love, rewatching all seasons of Friends, listening to Atif Aslam’s heartbreak anthems in a loop, and memorising Jaun Elia’s most devastating couplets, young Lahoris seem remarkably unprepared for romance in real life.
My anonymous survey confirmed it. Gen Z and millennials alike are largely paralysed by the prospect of modern romance.
A familiar tension kept surfacing across the responses I received. The inclination to date existed alongside a palpable fear of judgement and social consequences. Online discourse was cited as evidence; posts and reels on Instagram about dating can quickly become battlegrounds over what constitutes acceptable behaviour, with some commenters not merely disapproving of dating but calling for stricter boundaries in the name of moral values and “purity”. On the other side are those who defend the right to date, though often with a disclaimer attached: adults should be free to make their own choices, provided nobody is harmed. Even the defence of dating, then, is frequently framed as a case for personal freedom as opposed to an embrace of romance.
The Gen Z and millennials have been subjected to relentless messaging from both progressive and traditional benches, which puts dating at an intriguing intersection of two irreconcilable realities. Modern psychology and liberal education tells them to set boundaries and be the CEO of their own love life. Pakistani family culture tells them those boundaries are a sin. Caught in the crossfire, Lahoris are perpetually oscillating between self-actualisation and filial duty, paying the emotional tax of whichever voice screams the loudest.
To the traditionalists, any line crossed between men and women—whether a fleeting friendship or a casual date (what some would call a situationship these days)—is tagged as a moral liability. According to them, the rise in domestic violence, messy divorces, and infidelity traces straight back to liberal schooling, the lawless noise of social media, and the erasure of gender boundaries.
Flip the coin, and the progressives see the exact same horrors. The abuse, the fractured marriages, the betrayal, and the senseless murder of women, as the grim byproduct of missing liberal values and a culture that starves men and women of normal, healthy dialogue.
But even in the polished pockets of Lahore where dating is rather normalised, the reality on the ground isn’t as straightforward. Anonymised accounts from those who have dated/are currently dating in the city, noted a sense of inherent paranoia. On the streets, it’s a constant dodge of prying eyes and predatory police. Inside the hip cafes, the romantic mood competes with the cold sting of overpriced Spanish lattes and fettuccine.
The anxieties of modern dating take different shapes depending on who you ask. For women, the stakes scale up drastically. A single slip-up, a spotted outing by a relative, jeopardises their access to education, career, and in many cases, basic mobility. One woman shared her fear of being doxxed wherein her intimate photos and private texts could be weaponised across social media. Another admitted to fearing that a bitter ex might resurface after marriage to destroy her future. A segment of women answered that they constantly grapple with ingrained religious guilt. For most though, the core fear was far more immediate. It was confronting the entrenched patriarchal mindsets of their own families, where dating risked public dishonour.
For young couples, a simple moment of holding hands in a parked car carries the threat of police shakedowns and extortion. Worse still, the constant stream of news headlines reporting violence against dating partners leaves many terrified of the very people they are meeting. When things turn dangerous, the closeted nature of these relationships cuts off all escape routes.
As always, the heaviest burden falls on women, who face a court of public opinion and a legal apparatus far quicker to condemn a female victim than her male counterpart, a double standard laid bare on social feeds after every fresh report of abuse or femicide.
And yet, across Lahore, people continue to risk their safety, reputations, and futures for love, intimacy, or basic connection. Whatever one’s moral stance on the practice, dating in this context is a privilege for a few, a calculated risk for many, and an outright liability for most. Still, against all odds and taboos, the daring spirit for human attachment remains.

item.content:encoded:
The Challenge star CT Tamburello is revealing new details about his surprising romance with The Real Housewives of Atlanta’s Phaedra Parks.
“I’ll say — I don’t want to jinx it — but I’ll say we’re in a good place,” CT, 46, exclusively told Us on Saturday, September 19, while walking the UFC 331 on Paramount+ red carpet outside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.
Phaedra, 52, shocked the Bravoverse and MTV world alike when she confirmed her once-platonic relationship with CT had turned romantic. The pair later made their red carpet couple debut while attending 2026 Creative Arts Emmys on September 5.
“It’s definitely the real deal, and they’re really smitten with each other,” a source exclusively shared with Us shortly after their romance went public. “They became really close on The Traitors, but CT never thought he actually had a chance with Phaedra.”
The couple met in 2023, while filming season 2 of Peacock’s hit reality show. Although the pair grabbed the attention of viewers with their palpable chemistry, which included Phaedra’s loving “castle daddy” nickname for CT, their platonic relationship didn’t evolve until recently.
“He always had a bit of a crush on her and was interested, but he really valued their friendship and never wanted to cross that line,” the source said. “After his marriage ended, he and Phaedra started talking a lot more, and their relationship naturally grew from there.” (CT and his estranged wife, Catalina White, got married in 2024. She filed for divorce in January but later requested to dismiss the motion. Months later, in June, CT filed his own petition, claiming the pair’s marriage “is irretrievably broken.”)
The source continued, “Most of their relationship has been long-distance so far, but they have made it work and travel to see each other.”
When speaking to Us on Saturday, CT opened up about the pair’s long-distance romance and why — for now — he thinks it’s the perfect setup.
“I know I’m crazy in my own right. It’s probably for the best if I’m not around her every day, to be honest,” CT dished. “But she’s amazing. She really is. The way I would describe it is like Paula Abdul, ‘Opposites Attract.’ You remember that old video? That’s us, you know?”
While the reality TV star is obviously giddy about his new romance, he told Us he has learned that some things are best kept secret.
“I mean, contrary to popular belief, I do learn,” he joked. “Maybe a slower learner, but I do learn, and some things are better left unsaid and I think oversharing can be a bad thing.”
One thing CT is willing to share, however, is the thing he appreciates the most about his new girlfriend.
“With her, she just brings peace,” he said. “It’s easy to just stay calm around her.”

item.content:encoded:
After years of captivating users with endless swipes, dating apps are now trying to get people to put their phones down and find connection in the real world.
Tinder, the pioneer of the dating swipe, is now one of the companies leading this expansion of IRL events. In March, the company introduced an Events feature in its app and hosted a pilot event for users in Los Angeles.
Since then, the feature has started to catch on, especially with younger people, said Tinder chief product officer Mark Kantor. The company since March has seen 71% of its Gen Z users in L.A. visit the Events feature on its app. Meanwhile, only 63% of users 25 and older engaged with it.
The company has now expanded the feature to 20 cities, mostly in the U.S. but also in Europe. The idea, Kantor told Fortune via email, is to shed the label of “dating event” and instead allow users to meet potential matches while doing something they already love like pickleball, trivia, or sauna and cold plunge sessions.
The company has partnered with several companies to facilitate these kinds of activities including City Pickle, Joust, and Othership.
“The activity gives people a natural starting point, and the shared experience takes some of the pressure out of meeting someone new,” he said.
Another established dating app company, Bumble, said it is also helping extend its reach beyond swipes and messages with events and activations. This year, the company has taken over bars across New York for singles mixers, hosted a rooftop party in Nashville, and held an event with Barstool Sports’ Tommy Smokes in Boston.
“IRL has been part of Bumble’s DNA from the start. We know that one of the biggest points of friction in dating today is the gap between connecting online and actually meeting in person, and we’re focused on helping close that gap,” a Bumble spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.
Outside of dating apps, Gen Z and other young people have increasingly turned to in-person activities like run clubs for a sense of community, and also for romantic connection. According to Strava, participation in run clubs grew 59% over the past two years. At the same time, Gen Z is drinking less alcohol at bars and clubs, to the dismay of the night life industry.
Dating app companies’ increasing push for real-world events comes as user numbers have fallen.
Tinder’s daily active users were down 4% year over year in the second quarter, which was a slight improvement compared to past quarters. Paying Tinder users fell to 8.5 million as of the second quarter, an 11.5% drop compared to the same period two years earlier.
Bumble has experienced a steeper decline, with total paying users falling to 3.2 million in the second quarter from 4.1 million two years earlier—a 24% drop.
Swipe fatigue
Partly to blame for these declines may be swipe fatigue. A study of nearly 9,000 respondents from reverse lookup company Clarity Check in July found that 58% of respondents had deleted a dating app because they found it “emotionally draining.” Another 44% said they would prefer to meet someone in a low-pressure setting rather than get to know them through a profile.
Breeze, a dating app based in Delft, Netherlands, was created explicitly to get people to meet rather than swipe. The company, which has a team of 41 and has raised about $7 million in funding, charges by date rather than subscription.
Each user receives only a handful of profiles each day. If two people match, they fill out their availability rather than opening a chat, and then Breeze brings the pair together at a partner venue.
“A short real-world date tells you more about compatibility than weeks of texting, and it does it faster and with less of the anxiety and second-guessing that endless chat creates,” Marco van der Woude, Breeze’s cofounder and head of business development, told Fortune in an email.

item.content:encoded:
Dec on Dave
What were you hoping for?
A sweet-hearted madman who would make me belly laugh.
First impressions?
Looked like a David. A bit nervous and jittery, but considerate, curious and chatty (all the best C-words).
What did you talk about?
People in cars shouting “ginge” at him. Us coming from the West Country (but only I sound like it). How I don’t like Clapham gays – guess where he lives?
Most awkward moment?
I tried on his stethoscope, pretending to listen for a heartbeat from the chicken.
Good table manners?
Sound as a pound.
Best thing about David?
His passion for his profession. Also, how he was so keen to ask, listen and hear.
Would you introduce David to your friends?
Possibly, so they can give him his second Buzzballz ever!
Describe David in three words
Moustached, kind, grounded.
What do you think David made of you?
Probably an absolute loony. No, I wonder if he saw through the tarty humour to my kind, smart, caring self.
Did you go on somewhere?
The kitchen was closing, and he had to work in the morning, saving lives – very inconsiderate.
And … did you kiss?
I gave him a polite peck on the cheek when we hugged bye-bye.
If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?
Nothing: it was the perfect balance of sincere connection and nonsense.
Marks out of 10?
A solid 6. He’s a cracking bloke and rocks a floral shirt better than anyone I know. It’s a 6 not a 7 because I don’t like fish or salad; he kindly ordered me both.
Would you meet again?
We swapped numbers. We’re not each other’s “spark”, but had a good evening.
David on Dec
What were you hoping for?
Someone who put me at ease, asked me questions and made me want to text my friends about him in the toilet.
First impressions?
Definitely a main character. Handsome, potty-mouthed, charming and equally clueless about tapas.
What did you talk about?
Dec’s love of swearing. Coming out.
Most awkward moment?
Possibly when I realised I had a child’s blood on my trousers.
Good table manners?
Impeccable.
Best thing about Dec?
He’s very free and at ease in himself, and made me feel I could be too. And his autobiography will be a bestseller.
Would you introduce Dec to your friends?
I would. But I didn’t toilet-text them.
Describe Dec in three words
Curious, beautiful, free.
What do you think Dec made of you?
Hopefully good company! “Doctor” brings a whole set of expectations, but it felt like he was able to see past all that.
Did you go on somewhere?
We didn’t – but we stayed until closing.
And … did you kiss?
A quick peck at the station.
If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?
We were side-by-side at the bar, which is weird for a first date. And he got my right side, which is definitely less good.
Marks out of 10?
8.
Would you meet again?
We agreed the chemistry felt more friendly than romantic, but I’d love to stay in touch.
Dec and David ate at Barrafina Drury Lane, London WC2. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

item.content:encoded:
I’ve just tried blind speed-dating. Missed it in my twenties. Was too square.
Now in a spasm of late forties’ angst I’ve spent hours calling total strangers trying to make them like me.
I didn’t ever think I’d end up speed-dating. Didn’t think the wife would approve – or that would-be girl for that matter. I’m a bit out of practice – and out of shape let’s face it. But after this week, like a 49-year-old virgin on a first date, I’ve become something of a silver-tongued suitor. Just not on the right people. I’m told girls love questions. It shows you care. But I’ve discovered that civil servants on the end of a phone don’t. Even if they’re called Shahida.
My wife Tetiana needed a share code. It’s an electronic ID. A random mix of numbers and letters the government gives you if you’re not a citizen so you can work, rent or, in our case, get a mortgage. They should just tattoo it on your arm when you first arrive at Dover. There’s an idea Nigel.
Now, Tetiana has been in the country since 2009. She has Indefinite Leave to Remain. Stamped in her passport – two passports ago. She’s allowed in even though in her fur coat she looks like a Romanian people smuggler. She can be let loose on a mental health clinic but she can’t vote. Then three months into the remortgaging process, our mortgage advisor suddenly tells us they don’t accept paper visas. Although they did five years ago. You need a share code.
How do you get a share code? First, you set up a UKVI – UK Visas and Immigration – online account. Then they make you shlep all the way to Croydon to give your biometrics. It’s deliberate. If the office was in Hove, no one would ever leave the country. But who would want to stay in the UK after going to Croydon? In reality, most people who go to Croydon for a visa never actually leave. Because, trouble is, once Rick Deckard has bagged up your blood, hair, toenail clippings and fingerprints, you’re in no fit state to go anywhere else. So that’s Croydon.
And then you wait. And wait. Now a mortgage has a deadline. If you think you’re clobbered by your interest rate now, wait till you go on the standard variable rate. We had until September 23. Where was our share code? Silly me. Who’s going to catch any Home Office civil servant worth their salt working in August? Or even in England. I started to look up by-elections in Scotland to help make ends meet.
So, deep breath, we decide to phone UKVI. This is where speed dating skills come in handy. If Ovid was alive today, he wouldn’t write about the Minotaur – that horned cow at the centre of a labyrinth. No. He’d write about UKVI phone options. Because before you get to impress anyone with your wit, you need to press number 4. Then number 2. Then number 4. Then number 4 again. Then number 2. There are more numbers called out than during a night at Mecca bingo. Advisors are more protected from foreign reach than our gold bullion under Threadneedle Street.
It wouldn’t be so bad if it wasn’t a different advisor each time. “Calls may be recorded for training and data protection purposes.” Not to actually relieve you from having to tell them your problem all over again each time. And that’s before you’ve got past security. How long is your inside leg? What’s your cat’s middle name? Someone suddenly speaks: “How can I help you?” Can I remember how to speak English? “My wife needs a share code.” I hope he can smell my aftershave. Can pheromones travel down the phone line? “Have you got a UKVI account?” “Yes.” “Hang on a minute.”
Something in his voice told me this potential lover would never find my wife’s electronic data. My wife and I decide to tag team. The music stops and it’s time to move on. By the end of the night, no one’s marked my score card. Not even the wife.
All I can say is Tetiana must have more experience kissing frogs than me. However she wooed him, it worked. She probably chanced upon someone on day release from some luxury hotel that provides all day breakfast. With the speed and grace of a concierge at the Ritz, it took this marvel of productivity fewer than five minutes to fix my wife’s share code.
You can order swarms of bees on Amazon but if the state loses your data, it’s like looking for a yellow Lego brick in a children’s sand pit. Pity help us when the replicants take over.
Alistair McNair is Leader of the Conservatives on Brighton and Hove City Council.

item.content:encoded:
As streamers go, Netflix has one of the very best collections of original romance movies. The streaming platform is the home of modern romance classics like Set It Up, the To All the Boys I've Loved Before trilogy, The Wrong Paris, and People We Meet on Vacation. Netflix's romance movies are known for having well-written characters that are easy to get attached to, as well as compelling dynamics and strong chemistry between these characters.
While Netflix has a number of romance movies that are pretty much universally beloved, it also has some truly excellent ones that have slipped through the cracks over the years. These movies have clever main premises, strong dialogue, and captivating romances. These are forgotten Netflix romance movies that are truly perfect from start to finish.
'Along for the Ride' (2022)
Based on the Sarah Dessen novel of the same name, Along for the Ride follows a recent high school graduate named Auden (Emma Pasarow) who goes to stay at her father's home in a beach town called Colby, North Carolina for the summer. Auden is very ambitious and academic-minded, so she's missed out on most normal teenage experiences. Auden is already starting at her dream college in the fall, so now, she has the summer off to catch up on some of the things that she has missed out on.
Very quickly, Auden gets a job, makes some friends, and starts spending her nights going on mini-adventures with fellow insomniac Eli (Belmont Cameli). Auden's father (Dermot Mulroney) is more interested in writing his latest novel than parenting either her or his newborn baby, and Auden doesn't know how to connect with his wife (Kate Bosworth), so she spends more time out and about than at home. As Eli helps her check off items on the list of things she missed, the two start to really get to know each other. Auden and Eli's nights together are a bubble away from the more difficult things in their lives, though, and they soon realize that these outside obstacles could threaten their new connection. Along for the Ride is a sweet and cozy summer romance, and it remains severely underrated four years after it was released.
'Someone Great' (2019)
Someone Great is a beautiful movie with a romance that takes place out of order. Music journalist Jenny (Gina Rodriguez) is preparing to move from New York City to San Francisco for her dream job, and her boyfriend of nine years, Nate (Lakeith Stanfield), has just broken up with her. Thus, Jenny's two best friends, Blair (Brittany Snow) and Erin (DeWanda Wise), decide to cheer Jenny up and send her off by all having one last big adventure together before she moves.
Over the course of one life-changing day, Jenny, Blair, and Erin all reevaluate their paths and love lives. For Jenny, this means looking back on her memories with Nate and trying to determine where it all went wrong. For Blair, this means attempting to finally break up with Will (Alex Moffat), her boyfriend with whom she's no longer in love. Erin, meanwhile, has found a real connection with her new girlfriend, Leah (Rebecca Naomi Jones), but she is afraid to actually commit to her. Someone Great is an excellent movie that divides its romantic storylines amongst its three leads, taking them each on a journey to determine whether they want to fight for their relationships.
'Candy Jar' (2018)
Candy Jar is a coming-of-age romantic comedy about two high school debate team rivals, Lona (Sami Gayle) and Bennet (Jacob Latimore). They are the only two members of their school's debate club, and they are competing to become the club's president in order to look good to colleges. When they are reluctantly made co-presidents, Lona and Bennet start spending more time together, and they begin to question their previous impressions of each other.
Candy Jar is a funny and sweet rivals-to-lovers movie that is perfect for romance fans. Lona and Bennet are the only people who really understand each other, but their similarities also act as an obstacle to their romance. Both of their mothers put pressure on them to be the best no matter what, and they both worry about the potential risks that compromising and setting their rivalry aside could have on their futures.
'Love at First Sight' (2023)
Based on the novel The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight by Jennifer E. Smith, Love at First Sight follows two college students who meet at JFK airport while preparing to board a flight to London. Hadley (Haley Lu Richardson) is on her way to the second wedding of her father, whom she still resents for moving away so quickly after his divorce from her mother. Oliver (Ben Hardy) is going home for a family event, although he's vague with her about the specifics. Hadley and Oliver immediately strike a connection, and they get to know each other better on the plane.
When a technological mishap prevents Hadley from saving Oliver's number after the flight, they're separated, and she is determined to find her way back to him. Oliver, meanwhile, unknowingly waits to hear from her. Love at First Sight is a really sweet and emotional movie that questions the possibility of the concept of love at first sight through the story of Hadley and Oliver. The two barely know each other, but they both take a number of risks and bold swings in order to fight for the possibility of their romance.
'Wedding Season' (2022)
Wedding Season is a fantastic fake-dating romantic comedy that follows Asha (Pallavi Sharda), a woman who recently both ended her engagement and left her face-paced job on Wall Street to work for a New Jersey-based startup. When Asha's mother pressures her to set up an online dating profile, she meets Ravi (Suraj Sharma), but their date doesn't go well. After the two cross paths at a wedding, though, Asha asks Ravi to fake a relationship with her for the remainder of the weddings that they both have to attend that summer.
Thus, Asha and Ravi go to the rest of the weddings together that summer, pretending to be a couple so that their families no longer put pressure on them. Asha, in particular, isn't looking for love, and is much more determined to prove herself at work. Still, though, she and Ravi start to really start to form a connection through their fake relationship. The only problem is, there is a ticking clock on their fake romance, and Asha starts to realize that she might not be ready for it to end. Wedding Season is such a fun and swoonworthy rom-com, and romance fans who love wedding movies will really enjoy this one.
'The Lovebirds' (2020)
The Love Birds is an action rom-com that starts with a breakup. Leilani (Issa Rae) and Jibran (Kumail Nanjiani) once had the perfect romance. Now, though, it's been four years, and they fight all the time. Finally, on the way to a dinner party, Jibran and Leilani decide to break up. Seconds later, though, they hit a cyclist with their car. The cyclist then refuses their help, and another man steps in and kills him with their car, pulling a confused Leilani and Jibrani into a dangerous conspiracy.
Worried that they will be blamed for the man's death, Leilani and Jibran decide to pursue the conspiracy and solve his murder. The more entangled the former couple gets in this investigation, though, the more danger they find themselves in. The Lovebirds is an absolutely hilarious movie with a compelling action plot and an excellent second chance romance, where Leilani and Jibran start to see each other in a new light thanks to the life-and-death stakes at play.
'The Half of It' (2020)
The Half of It is a Cyrano de Bergerac-inspired coming-of-age movie about a teenage girl named Ellie Chu (Leah Lewis). Ellie lives in a small town called Squahamish, and since the death of her mother years earlier, she helps her father support the two of them by writing her classmates' essays for money. One day, Ellie's neighbor, Paul Munsky (Daniel Diemer), offers to pay her to write a love letter to his crush, the popular Aster Flores (Alexxis Lemire). Despite her own secret crush on Aster, Ellie agrees to it, but the letter quickly spirals into constant texting.
The Half of It has everything: a beautiful coming-of-age story, a lovely and unexpected friendship between Ellie and Paul, and a complicated love square involving the two of them, Aster, and her boyfriend. The romance between Ellie and Aster develops completely through writing, with Ellie feeling conflicted over the lie that brought them together in the first place. Meanwhile, Aster believes that Paul is the one that she is falling for.

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps were already hard enough.
Now imagine spending weeks flirting with someone, buying virtual coins just to keep talking to them and maybe even getting emotionally attached…
only to discover your situationship was basically ChatGPT with a profile picture.
Security researchers have uncovered a surprisingly sophisticated network of dating apps using AI-generated personas to convince users they were talking to real people.
Apps including Dora, Romi and Doni reportedly used thousands of fake personas capable of chatting around the clock, sending messages and keeping users engaged , while the apps encouraged them to spend money on virtual currency to continue conversations.
And this wasn’t some tiny operation.
Researchers identified more than 4,700 AI personas, interacting with around 25,000 users and sending 2.36 million messages in just two weeks.
The whole thing was apparently built like an actual tech company, with growth plans, payment systems and tools designed to help the apps pass app-store reviews.
So yes.
Catfishing has officially received a software update.
At this point, before falling in love online, apparently we also need to ask:
“Select all the traffic lights in this picture.”

item.content:encoded:
Netflix is set to bring a contemporary take on romance with its upcoming Tamil series #Love, which will premiere on October 2. Produced by showrunner Soundarya Rajinikanth and directed by Balaji Mohan, the series stars Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi in a fresh on-screen pairing.
#Love: Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi starrer Netflix new-age romance to premiere on October 2
Set against the world of dating apps, #Love revolves around Tara and Matthew, two rival founders behind the dating platforms FOUND and Find My Bae. While the two have built businesses around helping people find love and compatibility, their own relationship is set to put their theories to the test.
The series explores the question of whether chemistry or compatibility ultimately matters more in a relationship, while also looking at how romance and connections have evolved in the age of dating apps, swipes, matches and unread messages.
Monika Shergill, Vice President, Content, Netflix India, said, “This has been a defining year for Netflix India, as we’ve deepened our investment in storytelling from the South of India — and #Love is a title we’re especially excited about. As we expand our slate across Tamil storytelling, this contemporary, feel-good rom com stood out as a genre and that was ready for a fresh, confident take. ##Love steps into that space with a modern, chemistry-driven love story about two rival dating-app founders who end up testing their own theories of love on each other. Director Balaji Mohan, together with showrunner and producer Soundarya Rajinikanth, brings a wonderfully playful perspective to the series, while Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi bring the central relationship to life with chemistry, warmth and humour. The series captures that giddy, unguarded feeling of falling for someone you never saw coming - funny, warm, and exhilarating to anyone who's ever overthought a text message.”
View this post on Instagram
Speaking about the series, showrunner and producer Soundarya Rajinikanth said, "What drew me to #Love was how effortlessly it captures relationships today without losing its warmth and emotion. Balaji has created characters who are ambitious, flawed and incredibly easy to root for, and Arjun and Aishwarya bring such a refreshing energy to them. It's exactly the kind of contemporary story we were excited to bring to audiences with Netflix."
Director Balaji Mohan added, "When we made #Love, we wanted to tell a story that feels like it belongs to today. Romance has evolved, the way we meet people has changed, but the emotions at the heart of relationships remain incredibly familiar and timeless. What I love about this series is that it isn't only about two people falling for each other – friendship, family, ambition and finding yourself are equally important parts of their journeys."
#Love is written by Nirmal Williams, with Sharada Subramanian and Shweta Chakravarty serving as co-writers. The series is produced by May6 Entertainment Factory.
With Arjun Das and Aishwarya Lekshmi coming together for the first time in this pairing, #Love promises to explore modern romance through the lens of two people whose professional rivalry could lead to an unexpected personal connection.
#Love premieres October 2, only on Netflix.

item.content:encoded:
Dating apps are in a weird place right now.
Culturally, people are starting to hate them. Whether out of personal distaste or for safety and privacy, more people want to return to the real world to find connections. But dating apps are still big business. Match Group reported net income of $613.5 million in 2025, up from $551.3 million in 2024 but down from $651.5 million in 2023. (Match Group owns Tinder, Hinge, and a slew of other dating apps.) So, despite the complaints, they're still making money, and a lot of it.
And the ecosystem is getting increasingly niche. There's an app for conservatives. For leftists. Farmers. Christians. Christian Farmers. The rich. The famous. People who like movies. Double daters. Freaks who use 4chan. And now, entering the field as of last week, the dating app for people who read.
You May Also Like
AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections
Tinder — top pick for finding hookups
Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups
Hearing that a dating app for readers now exists is, at this point, not novel. But what piqued my interest is that the app was being developed by Co-Star, the astrology app. Now that's novel. Beyond that, with the backing of the Co-Star brand and ecosystem, it commands interest among young adults who like astrology and are considered popular and fashionable, i.e., socialite New Yorkers and Brooklyn-based culture writers.
Readme is a book reader's dating app, and its mission is to match people spiritually, much like the classic "meet cute" at the bookstore. And maybe, just maybe, spark relationships where they don't have to expose their (male) partners for being illiterate.
It's a book-series-sized task from the Co-Star creators. However, from my brief experience with the app, I found it to be ambitious but not well-crafted enough to justify waiting for the next installment.
Getting started with Readme
Setting up an account is no different than any other app.
Users fill out their name, age, gender, dating preference, and what they're looking for. One of the app's two big hooks is that your queue of potential matches is built or can be filtered around your friends and people that are associated within two or three degrees of them. Kinda like old-school Hinge or Tinder's short-lived Friends of Friends feature.
Within the app, one of the filters lets you see only your friends, your friends' friends, or your friends' friends' friends. It's interesting in theory, in that Readme wants to replicate those meet-cute type moments that you read about in books. Not in practice, though, because none of my friends are on the app or know it exists. It just launched, after all. But maybe this is my sign to start hosting more parties.
The other big hook is the quiz that "uses psycholinguistics to explore the hidden links between how you read and how you relate," according to the app. It's 25 questions, with the bulk asking you to pick which of two quotes you like or dislike the least. After you pick, it reveals which author it was.
For example, some of the authors I got were Henry Miller, Robert Frost, Casey McQuiston (of Red, White, & Royal Blue fame), and Jonathan Safran Foer. The latter was personally embarassing cause I really, really dislike Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close, as a book and a movie.
Between the quotes are questions about your political beliefs, communication style, and the genres of books you like to read. The latter was particularly irritating because much of the copy in the app has millennial-esque snark that tries to be "smashpunk" but is just grating. I like reading historical non-fiction, and the closest option to that was "straight up facts." Another genre option was "the writing on the wall," which is so eye-rolling. Obviously, these are my own personal misgivings, but Readme somehow tries too hard not to be like the other apps, yet also wants you to know it's cool, hip, and too irony-pilled to be authentic.
At the end of the day, language like that is fine, but seeing "communism will win" and "nostalgic for Barack Obama" as options under "political beliefs" did get a laugh out of me.
Something not included in the questionnaire, or seemingly anywhere on Readme, is astrological signs. Nowhere to put my birthdate, time, and place. So if you're looking for astrological compatability, Readme isn't it. (Yet?)
After the questionnaire, you get a report on what your language preferences "reveal about who you are and how you love."
I got "Former Gifted Child" because I prefer metonymy over metaphor. The app's way of telling me I lack imagination. "You rely on structures and systems to make sense of the world," the app tells me. I wouldn't say it's wrong, because my parents always believed I was a precocious kid. Turns out I had ADHD the whole time, so maybe the app was onto something.
The report also details How I Love and What You Need. Overall, the report is neat but a bit basic if you remove the flowery language. I like the book recommendations it gave me, and it even gave me some questions I should ask on a first date. Per my ReadMe report, I'm a lover boy at heart and need someone who's not as rigid.
"You need someone who finds the social script so uninteresting that they haven't bothered reading it, and don't know or care whether they're following or breaking it," my report read. Sometimes it's hard to tell whether the copy was written by a millennial ad executive or by ChatGPT's poor interpretation of one.
Using the Readme app
So now that the setup is done, what's the actual app like? It's....fine. It's definitely a dating app. You click the heart to like and the minus sign to dislike. At the bottom of every profile, you'll see a similarity score based on their quiz answers and choices. And that's it, honestly.
The big glaring issue here is that Readme just doesn't have the juice yet.
Immediately upon getting to the app proper, my recommended likes all live in New York. I live in Chicago. There's no filter or setting for distance. The only settings you can change are age, gender, and mutuals. For me, the app is a nonstarter. Not that it can't be successful, but I live in the third-largest city in the U.S., and Readme's algorithm is only showing me people who don't live in my city. Maybe it should've had a limited launch in Brooklyn first, gotten some hype, and then rolled out to other major cities.
I swiped right on between 70 and 80 profiles in my selected age range (24-32) before running out of people to see. None of them was based in Chicago. I saw accounts from Vermont, New Jersey, Denver, San Francisco, and even Tokyo. But not one in 70+ swipes lived in Chicago or set their location as Chicago.
I guess on the positive side, unlike the big power players like Hinge and Tinder, you do have unlimited likes. It'll be interesting to see if that'll be the case as the app gets more attention — venture capital and vibes can only subsidize an app for so long. Maybe then the dating pool will keep me invested enough not to be on the app when the bill comes due.
To be frank, having a cis hetero male perspective on the dating app for readers probably doesn't give one a sense of what the dating pool is like. Statistically, people don't read that much in general, but women read far more often than men. According to a Pew Research Center study conducted in Oct. 2025, "women are more likely than men to say they've read a book in the past 12 months."
One can extrapolate from the many cultural reasons why women read more than men. I imagine the main appeal of an app like Readme for women is that avid reading can be seen as a sign of intelligence, empathy, and curiosity. With the rise of dudebro, Barstool conservatism in young men, an online dating app that, to an extent, filters one from an embarrassing partner, is appealing.
All of that said, this is from my perspective as a 28-year-old Black man living in Chicago. The aesthetic leanings of Readme's dating pool are what you'd expect from an app that markets itself as a zine-style, indie sleaze, Y2K vintage fashion store you'd find in the more affluent parts of Brooklyn. In short, it's very white. Which is not bad, and I don't mean to imply that there aren't women of color on the app, but as it's been researched before, dating apps' algorithms are not kind to Black women, or people of color in general.
It's a shame because its style and interface are easy to get acclimated with, but beyond the mutuals feature and the quiz, it doesn't really do enough to stand out. If anything, what sets Readme apart from the crowd of hyper-niche dating apps is that it knows and markets itself exactly towards the audience it wants.
That's fine, but it'd be interesting to see whether it can expand beyond that — if it even wants to.
Chance Townsend is the General Assignments Editor at Mashable, covering tech, video games, dating apps, digital culture, and whatever else comes his way. He has a Master's in Journalism from the University of North Texas and is a proud orange cat father. His writing has also appeared in PC Mag and Mother Jones.

Streaming details of Tamil series #Love
#Love will premiere on Netflix on October 2, 2026. The series will be available in Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, giving viewers across multiple South Indian language markets a chance to watch the new romantic drama.
At the centre of #Love is a question that has become increasingly relevant in the world of modern dating, should people look for chemistry or compatibility when choosing a partner?
The series uses the dating-app world to explore this debate. Its story follows characters who have their own ideas about what makes a relationship work. While chemistry can create an immediate connection between two people, compatibility may determine whether that relationship can survive in the long run.
Aishwarya Lekshmi plays a single dating-app CEO
Aishwarya Lekshmi plays Tara, a woman who runs a dating app but is single herself. Her professional life revolves around helping people find potential partners, but her personal life does not appear to follow the same formula.
Arjun Das plays the other central character. In the latest glimpse, his character questions Tara about her belief that compatibility is enough for a successful relationship. Tara argues that if two people are genuinely compatible, chemistry will eventually follow. Their exchange sets up the central debate of the series while also giving the romance a light and conversational tone.
The new pairing of Aishwarya Lekshmi and Arjun Das is another major attraction.
More about #Love
#Love is directed by filmmaker Balaji Mohan, known for his work in Tamil cinema. The series is showrun and produced by Soundarya Rajinikanth, daughter of superstar Rajinikanth.
The series is produced by May6 Entertainment Factory. It is written by Nirmal Williams, with Sharada Subramanian and Shweta Chakravarty serving as co-writers.
The makers announced #Love earlier this year as part of Netflix India’s slate of upcoming releases for 2026. Along with the announcement, the streaming platform released a teaser that introduced the dating-app setting and the romantic conflict at the centre of the story.
The latest announcement has now confirmed the release date and languages. For Aishwarya Lekshmi, #Love marks an important career milestone as her digital debut. The actress has worked across Malayalam and Tamil cinema.
Arjun Das, meanwhile, joins her in what looks like a different kind of romantic pairing for both actors. The series uses their characters’ differing opinions about love to build its central conflict.
#Love premieres October 2, 2026, on Netflix. The series will stream in Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Stay tuned!

Hon. Evelyn Anite has shared tips on how couples can successfully maintain long-distance relationships, revealing that she is currently in one herself.
Taking to her TikTok, the former Member of Parliament for Koboko Municipality explained that communication and consistency are some of the most important things couples need to keep their relationships strong when they are separated by distance.
She advised partners to make it a habit to communicate every day, including sending a message to their loved one in the morning after waking up and another at night before going to bed.
“Communicate. You have to always be transparent and communicate with your partner,” she advised, emphasizing the importance of staying in touch despite the physical distance.
According to her, couples in long-distance relationships should make an effort to remain present in each other’s lives because a lack of communication can create room for disconnection.
When you’re not in touch, out of mind is out of sight.
She also acknowledged that there are many attractive people who could potentially come into a relationship, but believes maintaining regular communication can help couples remain connected and committed to each other.
There are so many beautiful and good-looking people out there who are willing to snatch your partner, but if you keep in touch with them, they don’t get a chance to even think about other people.
Hon. Anite further cautioned couples against dishonesty, noting that trust is another important foundation for making a long-distance relationship work.
“Do not tell lies, because if you do, you’ll lose them,” she said.

item.content:encoded:
Claire-Louise Bennett has said she is fascinated by the ways we exist in other people’s minds, by what we become when we are reduced to an idea. Perhaps that is why her fiction is always filtered through a consciousness: someone obsessively searching for a way out, or for a place in the world. Is love a kind of compass? Can it give shape to the self, each time in a different way?
Bennett thinks it should, but she also believes we are increasingly preventing it from doing so. Dating apps are no help, she says. In her latest novel, the intense, labyrinthine and deeply interior Big Kiss, Bye-Bye, she asks how love places us before a mirror and reveals the parts of ourselves we would never admit are also there. And something like that can only be reached, as Anaïs Nin might have put it, through the mystery of what draws us to another person when nothing has been agreed in advance.
At her home in Galway, Ireland, Bennett, who is also the author of Checkout 19 and Pond, answers the video call. She is seated at an enormous table. It is covered with notebooks and crystal spheres. Nearby, she says, there is even a glass penguin. And the mug from which she occasionally takes a sip still contains some of the Yogi Choco tea she made for herself a little while ago.
Question. Big Kiss, Bye-Bye is a long conversation between two lovers that recalls both the obsessive prose of Thomas Bernhard and the stream of consciousness of Virginia Woolf. In that conversation, Xavier functions as a kind of totem, a looming presence against which the narrator defines herself, sketching an outline of who she is and making herself real. To what extent is love a kind of existential compass?
Answer. I love the image. Yes. Without a doubt, it is. I deeply believe that love is an existential experience. I read Alain Badiou’s In Praise of Love a long time ago and felt he was right about everything. At the center of the experience of love should be difference, chance and risk — elements that today, in a world dominated by app-mediated dating, are practically impossible. Today’s world encourages us to think in terms of compatibility. We look for someone who fits us, who reaffirms who we already are. That very conscious way of approaching relationships can be quite transactional, like shopping, because it forces us to define in advance what we are looking for in a partner, what we expect from a relationship and what our limits are. Love is the opposite. Love is the great revealer.
Q. In what sense?
A. Love reveals who we really are. It shows us things about ourselves we would never have dared to imagine, much less admit. That is why attraction that arises in real life has such enormous force and, at the same time, is so unsettling. Anaïs Nin was terrified of being fixed into a stable, defined personality. She wanted to flow, to be always transforming, and for her love, made that perpetual motion possible — that existential expansion. Her stories and novels show how intimate encounters can uproot you, turn your world upside down, take you far from whoever you think you are at that moment. What today might be dismissed as mere romanticism is, in reality, what makes love a deeply singular experience. After all, it is the most powerful force there is, provided one has the courage not to try to manage or direct it.
Q. In your case, writing itself also seems to function as a compass, a way of finding your path through words and through what words construct: fragmentary scenes, memories seen from a single perspective, disorientation, something mutable and therefore open to transformation. Would you say that’s true? What are we, really? Everything we might yet become, or everything we have been?
A. Sometimes I feel I do not have a self, at least not in a strict sense. What I am is a place where very diverse forces orbit — and sometimes conflict —: archetypes, psychic patterns, impulses and memories both personal and collective, and many other things. There is a huge part of what I am that is completely unknown to me. And yet I know those unknown elements exert a huge influence on my everyday life. It is tempting to use writing as a way to make sense of that chaos and learn to navigate it, but the satisfaction it offers is only superficial. That is not what I am looking for. Samuel Beckett said the artist’s task is not to clarify things, but to find a way to make room for disorder. I completely agree.
Q. Is that why your writing has this quality of being unreliable, of constantly transforming itself?
A. Yes. My writing follows a winding path, full of false starts, dead ends, and overgrown landscapes. And, every now and then, small clearings appear where there is a sense of respite, immediacy, and communion. The thing is, I don’t write to affirm anything. I write by denying, subverting, and undermining. And that’s because, although we need to place some faith in reality in order to keep on living, deep down I don’t believe that what we call reality actually exists.

item.content:encoded:
You won’t see a more concentrated instance of how funny and frustrating Ted Lasso can be at the same time than an overly long bit where Ted fills out his dating profile. In signature Lasso fashion, mundane questions are but prompts for Ted to run wild with his brand of mistaken yet sincere and wholesome wit. (And what a way to target me, personally, with references to Stephen Sondheim’s Company and David Fincher’s Zodiac.) It’s cute, mostly, until it gets embarrassing. I fail to find a more apt summary for Ted Lasso as a whole.
In the seventh episode of season 4, “Yes & Baby,” we finally take a closer look into the lives of the Lady Greyhounds. It’s a safe assumption that playing second division women’s football doesn’t match up to Premier League paydays, but the series makes a legitimate effort to show what, exactly, all the women have to lose if they don’t shape up and get butts into stadium seats fast enough. Meanwhile, Rebecca and the Richmond front office navigate the uglier sides of the football business as Dani Rojas’s scummy agent tries some underhanded negotiating. Coach Alice (Tanya Reynolds), now in the new year, learns the power of “yes,” while Roy Kent’s love life hits a serious juncture.
Then, there’s Ted. He has permission to date now, which he always had and didn’t need, but it’s meaningful to have the door open for him. But it’s been a while since Ted put himself out there. And have you heard? Dating sucks now. Sucks! Vox’s Today, Explained just did a whole episode about it. Ted’s walking back into the jungles after a lifetime of domesticity, and he’s frozen stiff by a questionnaire.
I don’t blame him. Imagine being Ted, a grown man on the other side of a decade-plus-long marriage with a kid in high school. Being asked to describe oneself in three words must be banal, mortifying, and not the least bit embarrassing. Which is why I appreciate the resolution the episode offers to Ted, and perhaps all of us in the trenches of apps and endless first dates. Before we can commit ourselves to someone else, it’s critical that we recognize our own worth and love ourselves first.
What a beautiful sentiment. If only the rest of Ted Lasso were as brilliant and graceful.
“Yes & Baby” is hardly a stinker—I’d even wager to say it’s a rather good episode—but it’s just another episode where Ted Lasso’s forward progress feels perpetually hindered by its umpteenth step on a rake. I was on board for so much of it. Really. Rebecca, Zelda, and Leslie’s cartoonish phone call had me in stitches (I need Zelda’s “KAHK-sacker” as a text alert), and the farewell between Roy and Dr. Beaumont (Laura Haddock) was genuinely moving. The latter reminded me how, after watching an early cut of Spider-Man 2, Chris Carrabba of Dashboard Confessional wrote “Vindicated,” a song centered on the significance of recognizing someone else. (“I am seeing in me now the things you swore you saw yourself.”) How apt the song plays in the end credits after Peter and MJ decide on a life together, no secrets or masks between them. No, Roy and Dr. Erin don’t capital-L love each other in the same way, but there’s genuine power still in telling someone that you see them.
I’m not even mad at the convenient resolution over the “Believe” sign subplot either. When the team sees Coach Alice taping Ted’s new sign in their locker room, they’re swift to a deep and callous cynicism that even Ted Lasso’s folksy superpowers seem powerless to fix. But all it takes is Lizzie’s adorable four-year-old to read it aloud and they’re suddenly motivated to, well, “believe.” (And win.) Their transformation comes from nowhere and it’s all very tonally maudlin—which is, let’s be real here, typical Ted Lasso—but it’s got enough of the show’s missing season 1 magic to sweep me away.
Which is why I am irritated that the show habitually resorts to eye-rolling zingers and punchlines. The whole two-minute stretch where Keeley helps Ted fill his profile runs the gamut of cringe to funny to embarrassing to impressive to cringe again. (And to not even play The Greatest American Hero theme over the end credits? Come on! Whack!)
I like fun and whimsy too. And I can appreciate Jason Sudeikis’s karaoke pipes. But having your middle-aged protagonist swear he’s “invited to the cookout” and is pro-pronouns... Man, it’s just exhausting for what is ultimately just a ninety-second gag. Nothing about this sinks Ted Lasso completely. But it’s discouraging how the show can be capable of wisdom and grace only to zap the air out of the room with weak grasps for—I’ll say it, I don’t care—woke points. At the end of the episode, Ted himself finds the three words to describe himself: “I am lovable.” That’s beautiful. That works. It’s amazing how little can go a long way.

Best Friends with Benefits Dating Platforms, Reviewed

AdultFriendFinder ranks among the largest adult dating platforms worldwide, with millions of active profiles spanning a broad, open-minded community. Its scale and long operating history make it a default starting point for users exploring NSA dating online.
Key Features
- Geolocation matching surfaces nearby members for faster casual meetups
- Live chat, video calls, and cam features support real-time connection before meeting
- Free registration with basic browsing; premium membership unlocks full messaging
- Mobile app available for continuous access across devices
Pros

- Inclusive of diverse orientations and relationship preferences
- Multiple communication tools beyond basic messaging
Cons
- Pricing details require digging beyond the homepage, so first-time visitors should check the membership page directly
- Explicit content runs throughout the platform, which suits members already comfortable with that format
- Verification efforts keep improving, though active users should still confirm details before meeting anyone new

AdultFriendFinder suits users prioritizing community size and communication variety over a minimalist interface. It works best for open-minded individuals comfortable with explicit content who want fast access to local singles. Anyone seeking volume and flexibility in casual dating will find this platform difficult to match.

Ashley Madison built its reputation on privacy first, casual dating second. The platform skips the public-profile model most dating apps use and instead runs on masked photos, untraceable billing, and a messaging system that never syncs to your other accounts. For anyone treating a friends with benefits search as something between them and no one else, this is the platform built around that exact need.
Key Features
- Photo masking blurs your image until you approve specific viewers
- Discreet billing shows a generic charge name on statements
- Panic button closes the app instantly and redirects to a neutral page
- Traveling Man feature flags members visiting your city short-term
Pros
- Privacy tools go further than most mainstream dating apps
- Billing discretion protects users worried about shared accounts or devices
- Traveling Man feature works well for local singles wanting low-commitment meetups
Cons
- Smaller day-to-day messaging volume compared to bigger platforms, better suited to patient users
- Premium credits add up fast for members who message often, so heavy users get the most value per dollar spent
Verdict
Ashley Madison suits members who rank discreet dating above community size. The privacy architecture is the actual product here, not an add-on, and it shows in every corner of the interface.
Meet-n-hook — Best for Fast Casual Meetups
Meet-n-hook strips out the profile-building rituals other platforms lean on. Sign-up takes minutes, and the matching algorithm prioritizes proximity and availability over long bios. This is a platform for people who want casual encounters arranged the same day, not a slow-build courtship.
Key Features
- Same-day matching surfaces active users within a set radius
- Simplified profile fields cut sign-up time to under three minutes
- In-app chat opens immediately after a mutual match, no waiting period
- Availability status lets members flag when they’re free to meet
Pros
- Fastest onboarding of any platform in this list
- Availability status filters out members who aren’t actually free right now
- Lightweight app runs smoothly even on older phones
Cons
- Smaller user base than the major dating apps, which rewards members in higher-density areas most
- Fewer filtering options than platforms built for detailed intention matching, so it works best for users who already know what they want
Verdict
Meet-n-hook earns its spot for speed. If profile depth and personality quizzes aren’t the point of your search, this cuts straight to who’s around and free tonight.
One Night Friend — Best for NSA Dating and Local Singles
One Night Friend leans hard into geolocation matching, surfacing local singles within a few miles rather than a whole metro area. The layout keeps things simple: a map view, distance filters, and profiles built around one question — what are you looking for tonight.
Key Features
- Map-based interface shows nearby members by exact distance
- Intention tags let users flag NSA dating versus ongoing arrangements upfront
- Free browsing with credit-based messaging for direct contact
- Mobile-optimized layout built for on-the-go use
Pros
- Map view makes local singles easy to spot without endless scrolling
- Intention tags cut down on mismatched expectations before the first message
- Credit system means you only pay for messages you actually send
Cons
- Credit-based messaging costs more per conversation than flat monthly plans, which favors members who message selectively
- Profile depth is thin compared to platforms built around long-term matching, since the format prioritizes speed over detail
Verdict
One Night Friend delivers exactly what the name promises. The map-first design and upfront intention tags make it a strong pick for anyone prioritizing local singles over a wide search radius.
Tinder — Best Swipe Matching Dating App
Tinder needs no introduction, and that name recognition translates into the largest active user base on this list. The swipe format keeps browsing fast, and the sheer volume of profiles means geolocation matching rarely comes up empty, even in smaller cities.
Key Features
- Swipe-based matching processes profiles faster than list-based browsing
- Super Like and Boost features increase visibility for active users
- Passport feature unlocks matching in other cities before you travel
- Free tier includes unlimited swiping with capped daily likes
Pros
- Massive user base means local singles are rarely in short supply
- Passport feature is genuinely useful for planning ahead in new cities
- Free tier is functional enough to test the app before paying for anything
Cons
- Broad user base includes people looking for everything from casual dating to long-term relationships, so intention matching takes more filtering on your end
- Premium features are gated behind multiple subscription tiers, which rewards users who commit to one plan rather than sampling
Verdict
Tinder wins on reach. If community size and geolocation matching options are the priority over precise intention filters, this is the safest default pick.
Bumble — Best for Women-Led Messaging
Bumble flips the standard messaging order: women send the first message in matches between men and women, with a 24-hour window before the match expires. That single rule changes the tone of the whole platform and cuts down on unsolicited messages significantly.
Key Features
- Women-first messaging rule structures every heterosexual match
- 24-hour match expiration encourages faster follow-through
- Bumble BFF and Bizz modes exist alongside the dating mode

Pros
- Women-first messaging cuts down on unwanted contact significantly

- Match expiration keeps conversations from going stale
Cons
- The 24-hour window adds pressure for members with unpredictable schedules, which rewards users who check the app daily
- Same-sex matches don’t follow the women-first rule, so the core feature applies unevenly across match types
Verdict
Bumble stands out for control over who reaches out first. For anyone prioritizing safety and message quality over volume, the women-first structure delivers exactly that.
Scruff — Best LGBTQ+ Dating Community
Scruff built its entire platform around men seeking men, and that focus shows in the detail: filters for specific communities, event listings for local meetups, and a verification system that’s kept fake accounts down for years. It’s one of the more established names in LGBTQ+ dating.
Key Features
- Community filters narrow matches by specific interests and identities
- Scruff Venture lists LGBTQ+-friendly events and travel meetups
- Photo verification badge confirms real, active users
- Global reach with strong density in major metro areas
Pros
- Deep community filtering goes further than general dating apps offer
- Verification badge system helps members quickly spot active, real profiles
- Event listings add a way to meet people outside the app itself
Cons
- Smaller user base outside major cities, so density drops for members in rural areas
- Interface feels utilitarian next to newer apps, which keeps the focus on function over polish
Verdict
Scruff earns its spot through specificity. For LGBTQ+ dating built around a real community rather than a filtered version of a mainstream app, this is the more established pick.
OK Cupid — Best Free Registration for Intention Matching
OK Cupid runs on one of the most detailed compatibility questionnaires in online dating, using thousands of optional questions to score match percentages. Free registration unlocks nearly the full feature set, which is rare among platforms in this list.
Key Features
- Compatibility questionnaire generates a percentage match score for every profile
- Free tier includes messaging, not just browsing
- Intention field lets users state casual dating goals directly on their profile
- Filters cover orientation, relationship style, and specific dealbreakers

- Match percentage gives a concrete starting point instead of guessing from a bio
